content: Impetigo is a highly contagious bacterial skin infection that primarily affects children between the ages of 2 and 6. However, individuals of any age who participate in close-contact sports, such as rugby, wrestling, or American football, are also at risk. The term impetigo originates from the Latin word impetere, meaning to assail. It is also commonly referred to as school sores. The skin is naturally colonized by numerous microorganisms, but when their numbers increase or the skin's integrity is compromised, an infection can develop. In 1880, Alexander Ogston first described the role of Staphylococci in skin infections. Earlier, in 1863, R.W. Dunn described impetigo lesions as irregular, straw-colored spots. The first reported epidemic of impetigo in nurseries occurred in 1989. Impetigo can be classified into several types. It is categorized as bullous, non-bullous, or ecthyma. It can also be classified as primary (arising independently) or secondary (occurring due to another condition). Another classification is based on the causative pathogen, such as staphylococcal or streptococcal impetigo. Non-bullous impetigo, also known as impetigo contagiosa, is caused by both Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes and accounts for approximately 70% of all cases. The infection spreads through direct contact with lesions. The incubation period is 1–3 days for Streptococci and 4–10 days for Staphylococci. Bullous impetigo is caused by exfoliative toxins produced by Staphylococcus aureus. These toxins, classified as types A and B, lead to the formation of bullae in the superficial epidermis. The primary causative agent of impetigo is Staphylococcus aureus. Non-bullous impetigo and ecthyma are often associated with Streptococcus pyogenes, which can act alone or co-infect with Staphylococcus aureus. Non-bullous impetigo accounts for 70% of all cases. It is essential to differentiate impetigo from other conditions that cause pustules surrounded by red skin, such as chickenpox, herpes zoster, erythema multiforme, scabies, contact dermatitis, discoid lupus, herpes simplex, burns, and necrotizing fasciitis. In 2010, approximately 140 million people worldwide were affected by impetigo. The condition is more prevalent in children and is particularly common in tropical and Pacific regions. Risk factors for impetigo include insect bites, cuts, and other skin trauma. Additional risk factors include high humidity, obesity, corticosteroid use, chemotherapy, malnutrition, dysglobulinemias, and leukemia. Handwashing has been shown to reduce the incidence of impetigo by 34%. The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) has not established specific guidelines for impetigo screening. If left untreated, most cases of non-bullous impetigo resolve spontaneously within 1–2 weeks. However, complications can occur, including post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and rheumatic fever. Patients with impetigo often have a history of recurrent lesions, immunodeficiency, or skin trauma. Symptoms range from vesicles to bullae, which may initially be localized but can spread to the trunk and extremities if untreated. Fever and fatigue are common symptoms prompting medical attention. Lesions typically begin as pimple-like spots surrounded by red skin, which fill with pus, rupture within 4–6 days, and form thick crusts. Itching is a frequent symptom, and impetigo is often associated with insect bites, cuts, or other skin injuries. The diagnosis of impetigo is primarily clinical, based on a thorough physical examination and detailed patient history. Visible findings may include bullae, papules, pustules, or ulcers, depending on the type of impetigo. Although impetigo is usually diagnosed clinically, laboratory tests such as gram staining, culture, and sensitivity testing can help identify the causative pathogen and guide targeted treatment. Imaging studies, including X-rays, CT scans, MRIs, and ultrasounds, do not contribute to the diagnosis of impetigo. However, in cases of recurrent impetigo, additional diagnostic studies may be warranted to evaluate for underlying conditions such as immunodeficiency, malnutrition, leukemia, or diabetes. The primary treatment for impetigo is medical therapy. Topical antimicrobial agents, such as mupirocin or retapamulin, are effective for mild cases. For more extensive lesions or cases associated with post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, oral antibiotics such as dicloxacillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, or cephalexin are recommended. Penicillin is the preferred treatment for impetigo caused by Streptococcus. For infections caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), options include doxycycline, clindamycin, or sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim. Non-bullous impetigo is self-limiting and typically resolves within 1–2 weeks, but antibiotics are often prescribed to accelerate recovery and prevent complications. Surgical intervention is rarely required for impetigo. However, a biopsy may be necessary in cases of recurrent lesions or when the diagnosis is uncertain. Handwashing alone can reduce the incidence of impetigo by 34%.
